FM has the "Capture Effect"- The ability for a stronger signal of two (or more) signals to be demodulated and make the weaker signal even more weaker, hence blocking it out. (Which is pretty handy if you live next to a tower with a lot of FM broadcast stations, and only want to pick up one. Also helps with noise.) text:
Just answering number one:

1)What if I apply a square or triangle wave to the input of a transformer instead of a sine wave?



You can't.

No, wait I'm serious.Let me explain:
In fact, a square wave can be represented as a composition of sinusoidal waves.Which means that you're basically applying a lot of sinewaves that together compose a squarewave.

-----
example:
lets say we have a squarewave of 1000 hz(1 volt amplitude):

by using fourier series we can expand it in to this series:

  square= 0.636*sin(2*pi*1000*t)+0.212*sin(2*pi*1000*3*t)+0.127*sin(2*pi*1000*5*t)+0.091*sin(2*pi*1000*7*t)+....

if you add infinitely many terms you get a square wave(series converges btw).
-----

that decomposition is very useful because capacitors and inductors generally only alter the amplitude and phase of a single sine wave at given frequency(which means they act linear for sinewaves).

now remember your transformer is made of coils(inductors) and resistors.

that means that we are actually applying all those sines to the transformer at the same time.but since they have different frequencies  they'll be atenuated differently for each sine. which  means that the output of the transformer wont be a perfect square wave.

it will be distorted.That's one of the side effects. the ouput of the transformer will attenuate more higher frequencies and less lower frequencies.

Don't get me wrong, it will work, but if  you're just gonna get some deformed square  out of it why not just use a sine that wont weird out of it.

My point is: No matter the wave function you apply, mathematically you'll be just putting a bunch of sines/cosines in your transformer.

Debojit Acharjee Just to get this straight. The wattage of a speaker is NOT what you're looking for when matching amps and speakers. 
Take a look at the spec sheet of the speaker and you will find it's sensitivity. THIS is what to look for when matching speakers and amps, because it says how high the SPL is when only using 1 Watt.
Lets say you have two speakers. Speaker 1 is 8 ohms, rated at 35 watts RMS and has sensitivity of 91dB/W/m. Speaker 2 is also 8 ohms, but rated at 100 watts RMS and has a sensitivity of 86dB/W/m. You want to drive the speakers at 106dB SPL.
This would mean (after calculations) that for speaker 1, you would need only 32 watts to get it at 106dB. And for speaker 2 you'd need 128 watts for also 106dB.
You see what I mean? You shouldn't look at rated power or impedance, first look at the sensitivity to match a speaker with an amplifier. Then look at impedance to make sure your amp won't overheat because impedance can't get too low.

text: The math that you used to create your output filter was very informative. However, if you try turning the music down, you will hear zero crossing distortion. This is because it is necessary to create a dead time to allow one transistor to turn off before allowing the other to switch on. The higher the clock speed, the more apparent the zero crossing becomes. When playing loud, it's more than 20 db below the peak, so it is drowned out, and sounds pretty good. You can't beat the efficiency though. This topology maintains good efficiency at any load, any amplitude. The same cannot be said for a linear output stage. If you do a hysteresis feed back topology, and do away with the triangle wave generator, you will have pulse by pulse feedback, eliminating any trace of zero crossing distortion. You will greatly improve signal to noise ratio, and greatly simplify the circuit. I wish I had a way to show you a basic schematic to try.

No, it's the class A/B amp that can have difficulty with common mode noise...
Class D is almost immune to it because the amplified signal is fundamentally "noise", that gets filtered by the LC to eliminate the high-frequency...
The noise experienced would need to be large enough to produce significant change in the maximum output power - and would only really be experienced at that point, however if the common mode noise signal managed to reach that input preamp (not so much the comparator), then it's entirely possible that would amplify the noise...

text: So... you don't have a 1uF capacitor laying around somewhere????  Gawd, I've got hundreds!  Typical 1st layer IC decoupling cap...  And why did you not wind your own inductor if you did not have the value?  Got copper wire?  Got a #2 pencil??  40KHz is WAY too high of a value for a speaker that will barely put out 10Khz.  I am just wanting to warn the peeps that might scale your schematic UP to a higher wattage...   :-O  Yes, you cannot "hear" 40Khz, but it can certainly cause your speaker coils to heat up (causing failure).  Locally, we had a church that kept blowing high wattage compression diaphragms.  Yes, you are not expecting ROCK CONCERT levels at most churches...  It was found that a signal at a much higher frequency was on the line (heterodyning radio signals). An inductor installed at the horn cured it!  At a nightclub it was determined that high freqs from a distorted "hi-hat" (cymbal) was blowing the horns out!  Yes, what you CAN'T hear CAN hurt you!  Remember, with a simple LC filter, you are calculating the -3dB cutoff point.  The response will be -3dB down at that point - and only a curve of -12dB per octave above that.  So, at 80Khz (4 octaves above human hearing) you will only be down 15dB!  If your Fc was 20Khz (with a 2nd order filter) you would be down to -27dB!  With a 10Khz cutoff (which would be "barely" noticeable to 90% of the population) you would be down to -39dB!!!   Your tweeter would be totally protected at that point!  :-)  AND, a totally useless waste of money to use silver clad copper wire in the actual circuit.  Silver is the best conductor on the planet BUT only 6% better than copper.  SO, with all other things being equal (i.e not getting into the boring equations) say that the resistance of a same gauge copper wire vs a silver wire -  at 100 feet.  Well, copper (being the baseline) would be at maybe 6 ohms (remember ARBITRARY number - don't flame me over this...).  The silver wire would be still around 0 ohms (or tenths - or hundredth's of an ohm) BUT in your circuit, we are talking about fractions of an inch - not a hundred feet!  PLUS, this is the high impedance part of your circuit!   Silver vs. copper vs. steel vs. aluminium wire would not matter at all (except for maybe their solderability).  (BTW aluminum can not be soldered - easily).  Remembner, what are the leads of your OTHER components made out of???   On the output side (low impedance - 4 ohm speaker) , if you were running a wire more than 50 feet, silver "might" make a slight difference...  but this all gets back to that "audiophiles hear with their eyes" kind of a thing...
